analysis.one_liner: Restores the 2004 start date for country-of-origin labels on meat and farm products.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Agriculture Committee, leaving the two-year delay in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Congress had passed a law requiring stores to label where meat, fish, fruits, and vegetables come from, but a 2004 spending bill pushed the start date back two years, to September 2006. This bill would have canceled that delay and made the labels take effect by September 30, 2004. It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and never moved again, so shoppers did not get origin labels any sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who want to know whether their beef, pork, or produce was raised in the United States or imported, and U.S. ranchers and farmers who compete against imported meat and could benefit from customers being able to choose American product.

how_it_helps.text: Moves the mandatory country-of-origin labeling start date from September 30, 2006 back to September 30, 2004, striking the two-year delay Congress added in the 2004 appropriations act.
The underlying labeling law already covered beef, pork, fish, fruits, and vegetables, so the delay was the only thing keeping the labels off store shelves; this bill removes it.

analysis.who_pays: Meatpackers, meat importers, and grocery retailers would bear the cost of tracking and labeling where each product came from, and those costs could be passed on in food prices.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory origin labeling imposes recordkeeping and segregation costs on packers, processors, and retailers, since commodities from different countries must be tracked separately through the supply chain; industry groups argued those costs would ultimately show up in grocery prices.

The delay had been written into the Agriculture, Rural Development, FDA, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act of 2004, meaning Congress had already voted once to postpone the program; this bill asked members to reverse that decision, which some would see as re-litigating a settled appropriations choice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is straightforward information — where their food comes from — and to U.S. producers a level playing field against unlabeled imports. The cost is real but modest: supply-chain recordkeeping that large packers and retailers are already equipped to do, and which many already perform voluntarily for marketing reasons. The bill is a clean repeal of a delay, not a new program, so the design is sound; the question was purely political, not technical.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2004, sent to the House Agriculture Committee, and never received a hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Rehberg and Rep. Collin Peterson introduced the bill on January 27, 2004 to strike the two-year delay and require country-of-origin labeling to be implemented by September 30, 2004.
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee the same day and requested executive comment from USDA two days later.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
Because the bill failed, the delay enacted in the 2004 appropriations law stood, keeping origin labels off meat and produce until September 2006.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpackers, meat importers, and large grocery retailers, who avoided two more years of labeling costs and kept origin information off labels; shoppers and U.S. ranchers gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Rehberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the two-year delay in country-of-origin labeling.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: USDA
against.what_they_did: The House requested executive comment from USDA; the department's views were the only recorded input beyond the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the cosponsor a Democrat, but with only two members attached, the record shows too little activity to characterize the partisan split.

industries.note: Origin labeling would force packers and importers to track and segregate product by country and would let shoppers identify and avoid imported meat, reducing the value of foreign-sourced product sold unlabeled. The 2004 delay they benefited from is exactly what this bill would have repealed.

Retailers would bear compliance costs for labeling produce, meat, and fish at the store level, and earlier implementation shortened the runway they had under the delay. Retail trade groups were among the opponents of mandatory labeling during this period.

industries.industry: U.S. cattle ranchers and produce farmers
industries.note: Labels let consumers identify and choose American-grown meat and produce, a direct benefit to domestic producers competing against imports, particularly beef. Rancher and commodity groups backed mandatory labeling.
